Pitch Occupancy.

Master's thesis · CPU-only computer vision

Auditing how football pitches are actually used

One frame per camera per minute, classified as empty, active play or maintenance, aggregated into a USED / NOTUSED / REVIEW verdict, then reconciled against what the facility’s booking records claim. Entirely on one CPU, with no GPU anywhere in the system.

Zero-shot, no labels
0.988
cross-venue play recall
Frames labelled
1,692
across 9 venues
20 cameras
2.5s
of a 60-second cycle
Tests
283
passing

The finding that reframed the project. A rule that reads only the clock — “if night then playing, else empty” — scores 98.4% on the labelled data, matching every model the pilot benchmarked. Class and scene are the same variable in this dataset: empty pitches are 98% daytime, active play 99% night. Accuracy measured here cannot distinguish classifying occupancy from recognising a place.

Everything since has been about building an evaluation that can tell the difference.

What the argument became

1
The evaluation was uninformative A colour histogram beat a deep probe under a random split. Frames sampled seconds apart sat on both sides of the cut.
2
The models were not the problem Across unseen venues the trivial baselines collapse — the clock rule falls to 0.219 — while the frozen backbones hold above 0.87.
3
The protocol reverses the decision ViT ranks first under the leaky split and last under the honest one. The choice of protocol, not the choice of model, decided which one looked best.
4
The models genuinely read people Blurring away the players costs 0.12 recall; removing colour or the frame border does not. So the prediction rests on people, not scenery.

Findings

The protocol reverses the ranking

Three evaluation protocols, three different winners. A reader following the pilot’s protocol would have selected ViT — the weakest generaliser of the three.

Random split — leaky

ViT 1st

Frames seconds apart land on both sides of the cut. Everything scores about 0.99, including a colour histogram.

Grouped by slot — honest

DINOv2 1st

ConvNeXtV2 and ViT tie at 0.4975, which is exactly the single-class floor: they collapse to the majority class rather than merely scoring less.

Cross-venue — transfer

ViT last

DINOv2 holds at 0.930 play recall, ViT falls to 0.869 with a worst fold of 0.500. The pilot’s protocol would have picked ViT.

A model that never trains cannot leak. So OpenCLIP, scored zero-shot on the identical test sets, measures what changing the test set does on its own.

How much human review buys a given reliability

Why it is a band

890 / 907

of DINOv2’s calibrated confidences are identical. “The most confident k” is undefined over most of the range, so the accuracy there is an interval, not a point.

What the shading means

Every accuracy those tied confidences permit. The solid edge is the worst case — the only bound an operator can be held to.

The trap in the curves

The two best-looking curves belong to the two models that never predict EMPTY: right on all 898 play frames, wrong on all 9 empty ones. A figure of curves alone would recommend them.

What a new camera costs, in labels

A new camera starts poor

0.36–0.51

macro-F1 for a probe trained on one camera, scored on the other camera watching the same pitch.

One frame nearly fixes it

~0.98

reached by every backbone from a single labelled frame of the new camera.

The dashed series is the finding

From five labelled frames, training on those frames alone matches training on them plus 775 from the source camera — on all three backbones. What buys the accuracy is having any labels from the new camera, not a large corpus elsewhere.

Read as an optimistic bound: a second camera on one pitch is an easier target than a new venue, and the target set is twelve distinct scenes.

More labels made the models worse

Not a scaling law — a sampling artefact, and a useful one. Small budgets are class-stratified; the full pool is not, and is dominated by one mostly-empty recording. So balanced sampling accidentally de-confounds, and the curve is measuring the confound rather than the labels.

What was trained, and what never was

The three vision backbones were never trained on this data. They are frozen, off-the-shelf pretrained feature extractors. What was trained is a small classifier head on top of their output, plus two small models further down the pipeline — 10,932 parameters against 200,836,224 frozen ones.

Two traps live in this stage, and both cost real time.

1. The pooling head nobody trained. Hugging Face exposes a pooler_output on these models; on a plain ViT it is randomly initialised and never trained — loading the checkpoint literally reports pooler.dense.weight | MISSING, and this inventory counts 590,592 such parameters on ViT. Reading it cost the pilot a false 38% score and hours of debugging a model problem that did not exist. Every extractor here mean-pools explicitly and every cached feature file is stamped pooling="mean", so a stale cache is rejected loudly.

2. Two of the three silently re-crop the frame. ConvNeXtV2 (crop_pct 0.875) and DINOv2 (shortest edge 256, then centre-crop 224) each discard 23.4% of the frame area — exactly where the letterbox padding lives. Measured cosine similarity between embeddings with and without that step: 0.886 for ConvNeXtV2, 0.961 for DINOv2, exact for ViT. ViT is the only one that sees what preprocessing produced.

Stage 4 — two more genuinely trained models

These are the answer to “so you trained nothing?”. Both are small, both are reported with what they failed to buy.

Gated fusion head RQ5

3 statistics → MLP(8) → softmax over K backbones
Trained · 6,974 parameters fitted
Question
can a router pick the best backbone per frame?
Ladder
uniform (6,915) → constant (6,918) → mlp (6,974), everything else held identical
Training
full-batch Adam on CPU, 300 epochs, lr 0.01, seed 42

Answer: no. It puts 0.71 of its weight on DINOv2 in every one of 7 folds and moves that weight by only 0.057–0.101 between frames. It is a learned constant wearing a router’s costume — and its weight correlates -0.65 with night, so what little it does route on is the confound. Against uniform alone it would have read as “the gate works”.

STAN preliminary

Conv1d(3 -> 16, k=5) -> Conv1d(16 -> 16, k=5, dilation=2) -> Linear(32 -> 3)

about 13 minutes

Gated at 30 real slots; there are 2. The code enforces that itself rather than trusting a note in a plan, and its baselines are trained too — tuned thresholds, median smoothing, a 3-state HMM with Viterbi decoding, a logistic regression on four summary numbers. Beating unlearned constants would prove nothing.

Stage 5 — trained on nothing, on purpose

Majority class

predicts the most frequent training label

The true zero point. Under leave-one-venue-out it scores a perfect macro-F1, because every held-out venue is 100% active play.

Clock rule

reads the lighting field, no pixels at all

Learns “night means a match, day means an empty pitch” and scored 98.4% — matching every backbone. The most uncomfortable number here.

Mean intensity

one number per frame (1-d)

How bright is it, fed to logistic regression. Day-or-night, learned rather than hand-written.

Colour histogram

coarse RGB histogram (48-d)

Turf colour, floodlight cast and composition. Cannot represent “are there players on the pitch” — and beat a deep probe under a random split.

OpenCLIP zero-shot

laion/CLIP-ViT-B-32-laion2B-s34B-b79K

Never fitted at all — 151,277,313 pretrained parameters and a fit() that is a deliberate no-op. So the same per-frame prediction is scored under every protocol, and any movement in its score is caused by the test set alone. That is what makes it the composition control.

Why the backbones are frozen

1
Sample size1,578 development frames across 8 venues cannot support fine-tuning 86M parameters. A fine-tuned model would memorise the venues, and the finding would be about these 8 sites rather than about the models.
2
It makes the comparison fairFreezing holds the representation fixed, so when DINOv2 beats ConvNeXtV2 the only thing that differs is the representation. Fine-tune all three and the comparison is between three optimisation runs, not three representations — the research question would change underneath me.
3
Cost and reproducibilityEmbed once, reuse forever: minutes to embed 1,692 frames, under a second to fit a head. This is the only reason 4 protocols × 5 seeds × 8 predictors, plus every ablation, was runnable at all. Freezing bought the experimental breadth.
4
It makes the headline finding legibleA leaked split plus a fine-tuned 86M network gives 0.99 and no explanation. A leaked split plus a 2,307-weight probe gives 0.99 and a mechanism — the probe is too small to do anything clever, so near-duplicate frames are the only available explanation. Which was then measured directly.

What freezing does not excuse. The backbones’ pretraining sets (ImageNet-21k/22k, LVD-142M) contain sports imagery that was not chosen and cannot be audited here. Freezing removes this project’s training leakage; it does not remove their pretraining exposure. A stated limitation, not a solved problem.

“But the backbone has seen your test set”

Features are extracted once over every frame, before any split exists, so the objection is the right one to raise. The answer is that the backbone is frozen and never sees a label or a split — embedding a test frame is preprocessing, mathematically identical before or after the split. The leakage is in the split, not the model: frames sampled seconds apart are near-identical, so a random shuffle puts the same moment on both sides.

Random shuffle — leaky

100% of the errors on this split had a near-duplicate frame on the training side.

Grouped by scene — honest

0% did. Same frames, same model, same head — only the cut moved.

Schematic, not measured: each pair of blocks stands for two frames seconds apart. The 100% / 0% figures beside them are measured, in near_duplicates.csv.

Preprocessing

Every switch, before and after

Each switch here is a hypothesis about what does not travel between venues — not a setting chosen by taste. So each one is shown as the frame the model actually receives, before and after, with how far the frame moved measured beside it. 17 switch values, one source frame, redacted before anything was drawn.

The order is fixed, not searched

Stage 1
Geometry
undistort → ROI → crop. Lens shape is itself a venue cue.
Stage 2
Photometric
standardise, CLAHE, gamma, saturation, denoise.
Stage 3
Resize
letterbox to 224×224, aspect preserved.
Stage 4
Post-resize
sharpen, blur — so their radii are in model-input pixels.

One entry point, used by both the experiments and the live pipeline. The pilot’s most expensive bug came from a feature path that differed between the two, so a variant passes options rather than reimplementing a stage. roi is absent below because no pitch polygon has been drawn yet, and showing a tile captioned “ROI” beside an unmodified frame would be the most misleading thing on this page.

How to read the three bars

Change vs baseline

Mean absolute change per pixel channel on 0–255, relative to the loudest switch. How far the frame moved.

Pixels moved

Share of pixels that changed at all, scaled so 100% means the whole content area. A letterboxed 16:9 frame is only 56% content — the grey bars never change, so 100% here is 56% of the square.

Frame area kept

Shown only when a switch discards part of the frame. The number the pictures hide: a crop is re-letterboxed back to 224, so it looks like a zoom.

Before and after, switch by switch

Ordered loudest first, so the switches that barely touch the frame sit together at the bottom — which is the point of the section after this one.

A searched margin on top of a near no-op is not a margin. denoise=25.0 moves the frame by 0.73/255 and touches only 15% of it — against 39.1 for the loudest switch, letterbox=False. Yet the search reports it at 1.0000 recall, +0.016 over baseline. Both facts are true, and together they say the +0.016 is resolution, not effect. search_resolution.csv re-scores every searched margin against what the fold sizes can actually resolve.

And the crops are the opposite trap. centre_crop=0.5 keeps 25% of the frame while looking, side by side, like a mild zoom. It scored the largest apparent gain in the input ablation — 0.998 play recall — at empty accuracy 0.000, on folds that contain no empty pitch to catch it. It had not learned to see play; it had learned to answer PLAY.

Blur costs 0.12 recall

At blur8 no individual person is visible, and recall falls from 0.960 to 0.840. The prediction rests on people, not scenery.

Colour is a net distraction

Grayscale improves both axes at once: recall +0.022, false-play 0.231 → 0.021. The only removal that lands above the floor.

Two helps make a harm

Grayscale and a centre crop each help alone; together they score below the untouched baseline and call 98.8% of empty pitches a match.

1,692 frames, and what they cannot answer

STAN needs about 30

One gap explains four blocked questions. No empty pitch exists outside a single venue. That single fact makes cross-venue three-class evaluation, the calibration study, the risk–coverage operating point, and the clean version of the leakage comparison all unanswerable.

The fix is not more data in general — it is full-length recordings from any second venue. A complete slot contains the empty periods before kickoff and after the whistle for free.

The confound, as the numbers actually sit

Class and scene are very nearly the same variable here. That is what makes accuracy on this data uninformative, and it is one fact rather than a general shortage of data.

Empty pitches are daytime

empty frames that are daytime
98%

All 494 of them come from one venue, and 98% are daylight.

Active play is night

active-play frames that are night
99%

So a rule reading only the clock scores 98.4%, and the confound — not the model — is what a high score measures.

Where the frames come from

4 slot recordings

2 slots × 2 cameras

One facility. The morning slot is almost entirely empty, the evening one almost entirely a match. This is the source of the confound — and the only place an empty pitch appears anywhere in the dataset.

66 highlight clips

10–14s each

Roughly nine venues, day and night. Every clip contains players (YOLO-verified, minimum 3, median 8), so they add venue diversity and daytime play — but no empty pitches, which is why the gap above cannot be closed by more clips.

Conditions not covered

Lighting

covered

Day and night, and the only condition axis the dataset has.

Weather

no field, no footage

Every frame is dry. No claim about precipitation robustness is supported by anything here.

Maintenance

6 frames

Unusable as a class. It stays in the taxonomy because the system must be able to abstain on it, not because it can be evaluated.

Searches

The best model on this task has no labels

375 prompt sets, scored exhaustively against cross-venue transfer and guarded by a false-play control. Images are embedded once, so a prompt set costs almost nothing — the exact opposite cost profile to the preprocessing search, where every candidate needs a fresh embedding pass and the search has to be greedy.

How the prompt space is built

Part 1
Template
the framing — a photo of {}, a CCTV still of {}. Mostly affects how the text encoder situates the phrase.
Part 2
Descriptor
what the class looks like, in the vocabulary a caption would use. This carries the discriminative content.
Combine
Prompt set
one descriptor per class, rendered through several templates and averaged — so a set is scored, not a phrase.
Score
Cosine
nearest class direction, on cross-venue folds, with false-play as the guard.

The top prompt sets

Descriptor for “active play”Templates RecallFalse-playBalanced

Ranked by the balanced score rather than by recall, because three of these reach recall 1.000 by answering “playing” more often — the false-play column is what separates them.

A searched prompt beats every trained probe, with zero labels. “people playing football on a pitch” reaches 0.988 cross-venue recall, above DINOv2’s 0.930 — which needed about 1,500 labelled frames. For active-play detection, onboarding a new site currently costs no labels at all.

The caveat is not small. The prompt was selected against the same folds it is scored on, and 375 candidates is a great deal of selection freedom. This is a development result. The locked final venues were held out throughout, so the honest confirmation — evaluate this one prompt on them, once — remains available.

Which is why the hypothesis tests use a different prompt set. H6 asks whether zero-shot lags trained probes, and a prompt selected on the same folds cannot answer it — a selected number cannot test the selection. So the declared set is fixed by position: the first descriptor per class, all five templates, chosen before the search ran and deliberately not its winner.

System

From a frame to a billing decision

Step 1
Sample
one frame per camera per minute
Step 2
Preprocess
letterbox to 224×224 — the same entry point the experiments use
Step 3
Classify
frozen backbone + trained probe → class and confidence
Step 4
Fuse
two cameras on one pitch, weighed by confidence
Step 5
Aggregate
the minute sequence → USED / NOTUSED / REVIEW
Step 6
Reconcile
against the booking record, with 3 evidence frames

Rules the system holds to

Never invent an observation

A camera that drops for a minute leaves a gap; a total outage yields REVIEW, not NOTUSED. No footage is not evidence a pitch was unused.

REVIEW never becomes an anomaly

The system may not convert its own uncertainty into someone else’s error.

Anomalies are per field, never per person

Attributing discrepancies to individuals adds no scientific value and considerable ethical exposure.

No verdict without its evidence

A verdict and the samples behind it are written in one transaction.

The system never bills

Output is decision support; a human confirms every anomaly.

Faces are redacted before publication

Two layers — person detection and pixelation, then a whole-frame blur floor — on every frame that leaves the system, including the ones on this page.

preprocess-search — 740 min, 66%augmentation-transfer — 65 min, 6%the other 44 stages — 309 min combined

One stage is two thirds of the pipeline. preprocess-search is 740 of the 1114 minutes, because every candidate configuration needs a fresh embedding pass over the whole dataset — which is exactly why that search is greedy and the prompt search, where images are embedded once, could be exhaustive. It is also why --check exists: on a laptop that sleeps, you want to know what is missing before starting a 13-hour run, not during it.

What can run when

Levels are computed from the declarations, not assigned: a stage sits one level below the deepest stage whose output it consumes. So level 0 is what a fresh checkout with the footage can start immediately, and the depth of the stack is the real shape of the dependency chain.

Amber chips are stages of an hour or more. A few level-0 stages read only a feature cache from data/, which nothing here produces — so they are genuinely startable first, even though they are conceptually late work.

Where the repository stops

These inputs no stage can regenerate. They are the boundary of the reproducibility claim: given the footage, every number in the thesis can be recomputed from this repository — and without it, none can.

data/cache/ablate_dinov2_full.npzdata/cache/clip_image_features.npzdata/cache/geom_probe/convnextv2.npzdata/cache/geom_probe/dinov2.npzdata/cache/searchdata/processeddata/raw/venue_01

A stage with a missing input reports BLOCKED, never success. A reproduction script that exits 0 having done nothing is worse than one that fails, so stages verify their own outputs afterwards rather than trusting an exit code — which on this project has twice not meant what it said. All 46 stages report their outputs present.

Running it

1. See what is stale

uv run python experiments/reproduce_all.py --check

Runs nothing. Reports missing outputs, stale outputs and blocked stages.

2. Run what is missing

uv run python experiments/reproduce_all.py

Resumable — the expensive stages pick up simply by running again.

3. One stage at a time

uv run python experiments/h3_cross_venue_recall.py

Every stage is also a script. Run the latency stages deliberately, on an idle machine.

Setup

git checkout feat/prompt-search
uv sync
uv run pitch info
uv run pytest -q -m "not slow"

The code is not on main. All 39 commits sit on a stacked chain of feature branches; the tip holds everything.

And do not pass --limit to the preprocessing search for a number you intend to quote. Subsampling shrinks the venue folds until recall can only take a few discrete values; the script warns when it happens.

Everyday commands

uv run pitch manifest      # rebuild the manifest, print confound warnings
uv run pitch coverage      # class x lighting x venue matrix
uv run pitch cache         # embed every frame per backbone (~25 min)
uv run pitch serve         # dashboard API on :8000
